catalog_locator: Chapter 3 Phonology, sec. 3.6 'Tone', thesis pp. 70-72; LII article sec. 6
catalog_quote: The language which has tone is a tone language opposed to stress language where a change of tone does not bring about any change in meaning. Tone languages are further distinguished as register tone languages and contour tone languages. ... On the contrary, in a contour tone language, to which Bongcher belongs, there are successive levels of pitch fluctuation, i.e., the various tones include some in which the essential feature is a changing pitch (Pike, 1948). Bongcher shows a two way tone contrast; some of the vowels are pronounced with the pitch lower than the average while the others are pronounced with the pitch higher than the average. The tone which is lower than the average might be termed as low or falling tone and that which is higher than the average as high or rising tone. The falling and the rising tones are marked as [`] and [´] respectively. However, the difference in tonal variation is to be understood from the context as well. Few examples showing the contrasts of tone are given below: FALLING [`] ... RISING [´] /lùŋ/ ‘heart’: /lúŋ/ ‘stone’ /nì/ ‘day’: /ní/ ‘sun’ /ìn/ ‘house’: /ín/ ‘drink’ /rìŋ/ ‘neck’: /ríŋ/ ‘green’ /làm/ ‘dance’: /lám/ ‘road’

new_statements.rule_in_words: Bongcher (a Halam variety) is analysed as a contour tone language with a two-way lexical tone contrast (falling/low vs rising/high, e.g. lùŋ 'heart' vs lúŋ 'stone'), explicitly classed as a tone language rather than a stress language; the description gives no location for word stress. Debbarma 2017 (Korbong grammar, ch.3 sec.3.2 pp.12-13) and Debbarma 2018 (Hrangkhawl, ch.3 sec.3.3) independently report two lexical tones (high/low) and are likewise silent on stress; Kharlukhi 2012 (ch.5 p.37) instead says Ranglong-Halam 'do[es] not have tone' and also says nothing about stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Chaudhuri notes tones do not occur on /ə/ and that the tonal contrast is clearer in monosyllables than in words of two or more syllables (LII article sec.7 / thesis conclusion); no stress-related exceptions.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical/word level tone on syllables in citation forms; no phrase-level prosody discussed. Variety: Bongcher dialect (Glottolog bong1300) of Halam rang1267, data from Tripura.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes the Bongcher variety (Glottolog dialect bong1300 under rang1267 Halam), fieldwork in Tripura. Corroborating tone-only descriptions: Korbong/Karbong (Debbarma 2017; a Halam sub-tribe of c.117 speakers, Khowai/West Tripura -- Glottolog files this grammar under rang1267 but lists no separate Korbong dialect code) and Tripura Hrangkhawl (Debbarma 2018; = Glottolog hran1240 'Hrangkhol (Halam)' under rang1267, distinct from language-level hran1239). Kharlukhi 2012's 'Halam' is Ranglong-Halam (rang1271), which she describes as non-tonal. No source opened describes stress for any Halam variety; Ranglong proper (the ISO rnl reference name) has only morphosyntax papers and tone-marked texts open online.

new_statements.quote: Five vowels and two diphthongs are generally regular across the five KC languages of Barak valley. These vowels show distinctive length except in open syllables where the vowel naturally surfaces as long unless occurring as the unstressed initial syllable of a disyllabic compound. [...] The minor syllables in themselves do not carry any tone of their own, but received tone from the corresponding main syllables. [...] CVVD syllable is associated with different tones. Saihriem and Ranglong show three tones (HL, LH, and L), while Hrangkhol has only two tones (HL and L)

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog record (Chaudhuri 2017: Bongcher is a contour tone language 'opposed to stress language', no placement): adds tone inventories and the incidental 'unstressed initial syllable of a disyllabic compound' remark. Identity caveat: the work treats Ranglong of Barak Valley (Assam) and four sister varieties, not the Bongcher variety of Tripura by name.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The Barak Valley Kuki-Chin languages (incl. Ranglong) are tonal (Ranglong: three tones HL, LH, L on smooth CVV(C) syllables, fewer on stopped syllables); the only remark bearing on stress is incidental: the initial syllable of a disyllabic compound is unstressed (its open vowel does not surface long), and minor (sesqui-)syllables sa-/ma-/ra- are toneless and take tone from the main syllable - i.e. prominence on the main/final syllable of such words. No dedicated stress section is visible in the snippet material.
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing visible in the accessible material
new_statements.exceptions: none visible; Chorei lacks an e/ee minimal pair in closed syllables (length, not stress)
new_statements.identity_note: Haokip 2019 describes Ranglong (Ronglong) of Barak Valley, Assam, together with Saihriem, Hrangkhol, Chorei and Sakachep; the catalog record under rang1267 is for Bongcher of Tripura (Chaudhuri 2017). Glottolog files Ranglong under rang1267, so the work is about this glottocode's language but not the Bongcher variety by name.
